title: EMS Operations
summary: Everything around the patient: the system you work in, getting to the scene alive, moving people without wrecking your back, triaging a bus crash, recognizing hazmat, and surviving the career.

lessons.title: The EMS system and who lets you do what
lessons.body:
## You practice under someone else's license

An EMT is not an independent practitioner. Everything you do clinically is delegated to you by a physician **medical director**, and the boundaries come from two places: your state certification level and your medical director's protocols.

## The four national levels

The National EMS Scope of Practice Model defines four levels. Each one adds to the one below it.

| Level | Core additions |
|---|---|
| Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) | Scene control, CPR and AED, manual airway maneuvers, oral airways, bag-valve mask, bleeding control. Does not transport. |
| Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) | Everything above plus oxygen delivery, suction, nasal airways, splinting, spinal motion restriction, tourniquets, glucometry, oral glucose, aspirin, naloxone, and assisting a patient with their own prescribed nitroglycerin, inhaler, or epinephrine auto-injector. Transports at the BLS level. |
| Advanced EMT (AEMT) | Intravenous and intraosseous access, IV fluids, supraglottic airways, and a limited drug list. Not used in every state. |
| Paramedic | Advanced airway management including intubation, cardiac monitoring and 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, cardioversion and pacing, needle chest decompression, and a broad drug formulary. |

The exact list varies by state. Your state's scope is the outer wall; your medical director's protocols draw the line inside it. You may never exceed your scope, and you may not exceed your protocols even if your scope technically allows something.

## Online and offline medical direction

**Offline medical direction** is written in advance: protocols, standing orders, and treatment guidelines. A **standing order** is the part of a protocol you may perform without calling anyone, such as giving oxygen to a hypoxic patient or aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain.

**Online medical direction** is a live radio or phone consult with a physician during the call. You use it for orders outside a standing order, for unusual presentations, and for any high-risk refusal.

## Quality improvement

Every service runs continuous quality improvement (CQI): chart review against protocol, case review of significant calls, skill and response-time benchmarks, and feedback loops back to crews. The productive model is a **just culture**, which distinguishes human error and system problems, which get fixed, from reckless behavior, which gets disciplined. A system that punishes every error simply stops hearing about them.

## The New Jersey system

New Jersey is a **two-tier** state, and that shapes almost every call.

- **BLS** is provided by EMT-staffed ambulances run by volunteer first aid squads, municipal services, and hospital-based providers. New Jersey EMTs are certified by the Office of Emergency Medical Services (OEMS) within the Department of Health.
- **ALS** is provided by hospital-based **Mobile Intensive Care Units (MICUs)**, staffed by Mobile Intensive Care Paramedics who respond in non-transporting vehicles, commonly called fly cars. They meet the BLS crew and either ride in or release.

The practical consequence: in New Jersey the paramedic usually is not on your ambulance. You request ALS early, you begin transport toward the hospital rather than sitting still, and you meet them on the way. New Jersey's system is built around the EMT and paramedic levels rather than the AEMT tier.

> **Key:** Scope of practice comes from the state. Protocols come from your medical director. You must stay inside both.

> **On the exam:** Questions asking whether an EMT can do something want the national EMT scope, plus the phrase "varies by state protocol" where practice genuinely differs, such as supraglottic airways, CPAP, and naloxone.
keyPoints: EMTs practice under a physician medical director's delegated authority, never independently.
The four national levels are EMR, EMT, AEMT, and Paramedic, each adding to the one below.
Offline direction is protocols and standing orders written in advance; online direction is a live physician consult.
Quality improvement works best under a just culture that separates error from recklessness.
New Jersey is two-tier: EMT-staffed BLS ambulances plus hospital-based MICU paramedics who intercept in fly cars.

checks.q: An EMT gives aspirin to a patient with suspected cardiac chest pain without calling anyone. What made this legal?
choices: Online medical direction
A standing order within the protocol
The patient's expressed consent alone
The EMT's personal judgment
checks.why: A standing order is the medical director's advance written permission to act without calling. Consent authorizes touching the patient but does not authorize a medication, and personal judgment is never the legal basis.

checks.q: In the New Jersey system, how does a paramedic usually reach your patient?
choices: As the third crew member on your ambulance
In a non-transporting hospital-based MICU fly car that intercepts the BLS crew
Only at the receiving hospital
By responding in a separate transporting ambulance that takes over the patient
checks.why: New Jersey delivers ALS through hospital-based MICUs in non-transporting vehicles that meet the BLS unit. That is exactly why you request early and begin transport toward the hospital instead of waiting on scene.

checks.q: Which statement about scope of practice and protocols is correct?
choices: Protocols may authorize actions beyond your state scope
Your scope is set by the state and your protocols draw the line inside it
Scope of practice is determined by your employer
Scope and standard of care mean the same thing
checks.why: The state sets the legal ceiling and the medical director may restrict further but never expand past it. Standard of care is a separate idea: how a reasonable provider at your level would actually perform.

lessons.title: Scene safety, staging, and the hazards that hurt crews
lessons.body:
## Answer the questions before you open the door

Safety is not a feeling, it is a set of answers. Before you step out:

1. What did dispatch say, and what did they not say? Weapons, violence history at the address, alcohol, drugs, a caller who would not stay on the line.
2. Where is my exit, and is anything between me and it?
3. Who else is here, how many of them, and where are their hands?
4. What is physically dangerous here: traffic, fire, wires, unstable vehicles, animals, chemicals, heights, water?
5. Do I have what I need, or should I be waiting for someone?

## Violence indicators

Watch for a person pacing or clenching fists, someone who positions between you and the door, shouting that gets louder as you speak, a room where everyone goes quiet when you enter, weapons in view, and dispatch information that does not match what you find. A patient hiding their hands, or who keeps reaching into a pocket, is a reason to create distance.

If the scene turns while you are inside, you leave. You do not finish the blood pressure first.

## Staging for police

**Staging** means waiting at a safe location until law enforcement declares the scene secure. Stage out of sight of the address, typically a block or more away, not in the driveway. Violence, weapons, active assaults, unknown-cause shootings, and many overdose calls get staged by policy.

Remember that "police on scene" is not the same as "scene secure." Ask for the words. And a scene can become unsafe again after it was cleared, when a suspect returns or a family member arrives.

## Traffic: the hazard that kills the most crews

Roadway incidents are a leading cause of EMS deaths, and most of them happen to people standing outside the vehicle.

- Park so the ambulance shields the work area, roughly **100 feet** before the scene with the wheels turned away from responders, or past it if fire is already blocking.
- Wear a high-visibility vest meeting ANSI class 2 or higher. On federal-aid highways this is a federal requirement, not a suggestion.
- Work from the side away from moving traffic, and never turn your back to it.
- At night, use scene lighting on the work area but avoid blinding oncoming drivers with unnecessary forward-facing lights.

## Other scene hazards

**Downed wires.** Assume every wire is live. Stay back **at least one full span**, meaning pole to pole in every direction, and let the utility company declare it de-energized. Never move a wire with anything. If a wire touches a vehicle, tell occupants to stay inside.

**Unstable vehicles.** A car on its side or roof, or on a slope, must be stabilized with cribbing and chocks before anyone climbs in. Turn the ignition off, set the brake, and stay clear of undeployed airbags.

**Fire and confined spaces.** Interior firefighting, confined space, trench, and water rescue all require specialized training and equipment. At the awareness level your job is to recognize it, stay out, and call the right team.

**Animals.** Ask for dogs to be secured in another room before you enter, every time, even when the owner says the dog is friendly.

> **Trap:** The most dangerous moment on a roadway call is the walk between the ambulance and the patient, because you are focused on the patient and not on traffic. Look before every step into a lane.

> **On shift:** Body armor policy varies by service. What does not vary is that you do not enter an active violence scene, ever, and that includes an active shooter scene until a rescue task force structure and law enforcement escort are in place.
keyPoints: Answer the safety questions before leaving the vehicle: exits, people, hazards, resources.
Stage out of sight until police say the scene is secure, and remember police present does not mean secure.
Park about 100 feet before a roadway scene to shield the work area, and wear an ANSI class 2 or higher vest.
Stay at least one full pole-to-pole span from downed wires and let the utility de-energize them.
Stabilize unstable vehicles before entry, and have dogs secured before you go in.

checks.q: You are dispatched to a stabbing with police en route. What should you do?
choices: Respond directly and begin care
Stage a safe distance away until police advise the scene is secure
Enter with your partner but leave the doors open
Wait in the driveway with the lights off
checks.why: Violent scenes are staged out of sight until law enforcement declares them secure. The driveway is still the scene, and an open door does not protect you from the person who caused the stabbing.

checks.q: A power line is down across a car with two occupants inside who appear uninjured. What do you tell them?
choices: Get out quickly and run to you
Stay inside the vehicle until the utility de-energizes the line
Step out slowly with both feet together
Climb out through the sunroof
checks.why: The vehicle body carries current around the occupants, so inside is the safest place until power is confirmed off. Any exit risks completing a circuit through the body or crossing an energized ground gradient.

lessons.title: Lifting and moving without destroying your back
lessons.body:
## Why back injuries end EMS careers

The spine tolerates compression well and tolerates a bent, twisted, loaded position badly. Every inch you hold weight away from your body multiplies the force on the lumbar discs, which is why a 40-pound bag at arm's length hurts more than a 100-pound patient held close.

That single fact generates every rule below.

## Body mechanics and the power lift

- Feet about shoulder width apart, flat on the ground
- Back straight and **locked in a slight inward curve**, not rounded
- Bend at the hips and knees, not the waist
- Weight as close to your body as possible
- Lift with the legs, pushing the ground away, exhaling as you lift
- **Never twist while lifting.** Move your feet to turn.
- Communicate: count out loud, and one person calls the lift

Use a **power grip**: palms up, hands about 10 inches apart, with the full palm and all fingers in contact with the handle. The grip that uses only fingertips fails first.

Other rules that save you: push rather than pull whenever you can, keep the load between knee and waist height, and take shorter steps when carrying. When the load exceeds what two people can safely handle, call for a lift assist. Knowing your limit is a skill, not a weakness.

## Three categories of move

**Emergency move.** Immediate danger justifies accepting the risk of moving a patient before assessment or immobilization. Use it when there is fire or the threat of explosion, uncontrolled hazardous materials, an inability to protect the patient from other hazards, an inability to reach other patients who need lifesaving care, or a position that makes lifesaving care impossible, such as a patient in cardiac arrest on a soft bed.

Techniques: **clothes drag** (grasp the shirt behind the neck and pull, supporting the head with your forearms), **blanket drag**, shoulder or forearm drag, firefighter's carry, and one- or two-person assists. Drag along the long axis of the body to protect the spine as much as possible.

**Urgent move.** The patient's condition, not the scene, demands speed: altered mental status, inadequate breathing, or shock. Rapid extrication from a vehicle is the classic example, performed with manual spinal stabilization and usually three or more providers.

**Non-urgent move.** No threat and a stable patient, so you take your time and pick the gentlest technique.

## Non-urgent techniques

- **Direct ground lift.** Two or three providers, used for a supine patient with no suspected spinal injury.
- **Extremity lift.** One provider at the arms and one at the knees, for a patient with no spinal or extremity injury.
- **Direct carry.** Bed to stretcher, two providers, for a supine patient with no spinal injury.
- **Draw sheet method.** The sheet under the patient is used to slide them from bed to stretcher. Easiest on your back, and the standard in hospitals.

## Devices

**Wheeled stretcher** for most transports; roll it rather than carry it whenever possible. **Stair chair** for a conscious patient going down stairs, with a strap system and a spotter below. **Scoop stretcher** splits lengthwise and reassembles under a patient with minimal movement. **Long backboard** is a movement and extrication device, not a treatment; patients are removed from it promptly because it causes pressure injuries and interferes with breathing. **Basket or Stokes** stretcher for rough terrain, **flexible stretcher** for tight spaces, **vacuum mattress** for a full-body splint.

> **Key:** Move before you assess only when a hazard or a needed lifesaving intervention makes staying put worse than moving.

> **Trap:** Never carry a patient down stairs on a wheeled stretcher. Use the stair chair, and always have a spotter below the crew.
keyPoints: Load close to the body, back locked, lift with the legs, and never twist while lifting.
Power grip: palms up, hands about 10 inches apart, full palm contact.
Emergency move is for scene danger, urgent move is for patient condition, non-urgent is for stable patients.
Non-urgent techniques: direct ground lift, extremity lift, direct carry, draw sheet.
The long backboard is a movement device, not a treatment, and the stair chair is the tool for stairs.

checks.q: A car is on fire and the driver is unresponsive but breathing. What type of move is indicated?
choices: Non-urgent move with full spinal immobilization
Emergency move using a clothes or blanket drag
Urgent move with a scoop stretcher
No move until fire suppression is complete
checks.why: Fire is an immediate life threat, which justifies an emergency move despite the spinal risk. Waiting for suppression or setting up a scoop both cost time the patient does not have.

checks.q: You must move a stable patient from a hospital bed to your stretcher. Which technique is easiest on your back?
choices: Direct ground lift
Draw sheet slide
Extremity lift
Firefighter's carry
checks.why: The draw sheet lets you slide rather than lift, which keeps the load low and close. Ground lifts and extremity lifts both require lifting the full weight, and a firefighter's carry is an emergency technique.

checks.q: Which statement about the power lift is correct?
choices: Round the back to engage the larger muscles
Hold the load at arm's length for balance
Keep the load close, lift with the legs, and turn by moving your feet
Twist at the waist to transfer the patient sideways
checks.why: Force on the lumbar discs rises with distance from the body, and twisting under load is the classic injury mechanism. A rounded back removes the spine's protective curve and loads the discs unevenly.

lessons.title: Ambulance operations, driving, and air medical
lessons.body:
## The nine phases of a call

Preparation, dispatch, en route, arrival and size-up, transferring the patient to the ambulance, transport, delivery at the facility, en route back, and the post-run phase of cleaning and restocking. The first and last phases are the ones people skip, and they are the reason equipment fails at 3 a.m.

## The daily check

Do it at the start of every shift, before the first call, and document it.

- **Vehicle:** fuel, oil and coolant, tires and pressure, brakes, wipers, all lights, siren, horn, mirrors
- **Communications:** portable and mobile radios, spare batteries, phone
- **Oxygen:** main cylinder and portables. Replace a portable at or below `500 psi`; a full D cylinder starts around `2000 psi`
- **Airway and suction:** suction pulls at least `300 mmHg`, all sizes of airways, bag-valve masks in adult, child, and infant
- **AED:** self-test passed, pads present and not expired, spare pads
- **Bags:** jump bag, trauma bag, glucometer with strips in date, all medications in date
- **Stretcher:** straps, wheels, locks, and the loading system

## Driving is the most dangerous thing you do

Emergency lights and sirens grant you **exemptions**, such as proceeding past a red light after stopping, but they never grant **immunity**. The legal standard is **due regard** for the safety of everyone else, and a crash while responding will be measured against it.

The honest numbers: studies of lights-and-siren response consistently find a time saving of only about **1.7 to 3.6 minutes** on a typical call, while crash risk rises substantially. For most patients that trade is a bad one, which is why many systems have cut emergency response and transport dramatically.

**Intersections** are where ambulances crash. The rules that prevent it:

- Come to a **complete stop** at every red light and stop sign, even with lights and siren
- Clear the intersection **lane by lane**, making eye contact with stopped drivers
- Change the siren tone as you approach, because a steady tone becomes background noise
- Assume nobody hears you. Modern cars are sealed, insulated, and loud inside
- Watch for the **wake effect**: crashes caused behind you by drivers reacting to your passage

**Backing** causes a large share of ambulance collisions. Always use a spotter at the rear corner, in your mirror, with agreed hand signals. If you have no spotter, get out and look before backing, every time. Stop the moment you lose sight of the spotter.

Other essentials: everyone belted, including the provider in the patient compartment whenever possible; all equipment secured, because a loose monitor is a projectile; no distracted driving; and speed that matches conditions rather than the posted limit.

## Air medical

**When to call:** ground transport time to the appropriate center is excessive, prolonged extrication is expected, terrain or traffic makes ground transport impractical, multiple critical patients exceed ground resources, or the patient needs a specialty center such as trauma, burn, or pediatric care that is far away. Weather, aircraft availability, and patient size all rule it out sometimes, so always have a ground plan.

**Landing zone setup:**

- **100 by 100 feet** for most helicopters, on firm, level ground with a slope under about 8 degrees
- Clear of wires, poles, trees, signs, and loose debris; wires are the single biggest hazard and the hardest to see from the air
- Mark the corners with weighted cones or secured lights, never anything that can blow into the rotor
- Secure or remove loose items within 100 feet, including sheets, hats, and traffic cones
- Give the pilot wind direction, obstacles, and the surface type by radio
- **Never approach until the crew signals you**, always approach from the front in the pilot's line of sight, and never go near the tail rotor
- On a slope, approach from the **downhill** side, where the main rotor is highest

> **Key:** Lights and sirens save minutes, not lives, on most calls. Due regard is the legal standard and a complete stop at every red light is the practical one.

> **On the exam:** Landing zone questions want 100 by 100 feet, hazards identified, approach only when signaled, from the front, never toward the tail.
keyPoints: Nine phases of a call; preparation and post-run are the ones that get skipped and cause failures later.
Replace portable oxygen cylinders at or below 500 psi; suction should generate at least 300 mmHg.
Lights and sirens give exemptions, not immunity; the legal standard is due regard.
Come to a complete stop at every red light and clear intersections lane by lane.
Landing zone is 100 by 100 feet, approach only when signaled, from the front, never near the tail rotor.

checks.q: Approaching a red light with lights and siren on, what must you do?
choices: Slow slightly and proceed if traffic appears stopped
Come to a complete stop and clear the intersection lane by lane
Increase siren volume and continue through
Proceed at posted speed since you have right of way
checks.why: Emergency exemptions require due regard, and intersections are where ambulances crash. Drivers in sealed modern cars frequently do not hear a siren, so a full stop and lane-by-lane clearing is the only reliable approach.

checks.q: You are setting up a landing zone in a field. Which is the correct size and priority hazard?
choices: 60 by 60 feet, with pedestrians as the main hazard
100 by 100 feet, with overhead wires as the main hazard
50 by 50 feet, with slope as the main hazard
200 by 200 feet, with noise as the main hazard
checks.why: Most helicopters need about 100 by 100 feet, and wires are the hardest hazard to see from the air and the most lethal. Slope and bystanders matter too, but wires are the priority you must report by radio.

checks.q: How much time does a lights-and-siren response typically save?
choices: About 1.7 to 3.6 minutes
About 10 to 15 minutes
Over 20 minutes
It varies so widely that no estimate exists
checks.why: Multiple studies converge on a saving of only a few minutes, which rarely changes outcome while measurably raising crash risk. That evidence is why many systems now restrict emergency response and transport to specific criteria.

lessons.title: Extrication: your job and fire's job
lessons.body:
## Two kinds of access

**Simple access** requires no tools. Try every door handle, try the rear doors, roll down or ask an occupant to lower a window, unlock through an open window, and ask the patient to unlock. New providers skip this constantly and wait for a tool that was never needed.

**Complex access** requires tools and training: cutting a door, removing a roof, displacing a dash, breaching a windshield, stabilizing a vehicle on its side. That is the fire department's job. Your job is the patient inside while they work.

## The sequence

In practice a vehicle extrication runs in this order:

1. Size up the scene and the number of patients
2. Control hazards: traffic, fuel, fire, battery, airbags
3. Stabilize the vehicle with cribbing, chocks, and struts
4. Gain access, simple before complex
5. Provide patient care inside the vehicle, with a provider assigned to the patient throughout
6. Disentangle: remove the vehicle from the patient, not the patient from the vehicle
7. Package and remove
8. Transport

That sixth item is the mental shift that matters. You do not pull a trapped patient out through a small hole. You wait while the hole becomes big enough that they can be moved in a straight line with their spine supported.

## Protecting the patient during cutting

While fire works, you: hold manual in-line stabilization, apply a cervical collar when indicated, give the patient eye protection and hearing protection, cover them with a heavy blanket or hard protection before glass is broken, explain what each noise will be before it happens, and keep taking vitals. Noise and glass are terrifying from the inside, and narrating the process is real patient care.

## When you skip the careful version

**Rapid extrication** takes a patient out in under a minute with manual stabilization and no board inside the vehicle. It is indicated in three situations only:

1. The scene is unsafe, such as fire, fuel, or unstable vehicle position
2. The patient's condition is unstable and requires immediate transport
3. The patient blocks access to another, more critically injured patient

It requires at least three providers: one maintaining head stabilization, and two moving the patient as a unit onto a board or stretcher. It accepts a small amount of spinal risk to buy a large amount of time, and it is the wrong choice for a stable patient who is merely uncomfortable.

## Hazards specific to vehicles

**Airbags.** An undeployed airbag can fire during extrication. Stay out of the deployment path, do not place your body or equipment between the airbag and the patient, and disconnecting the battery is part of the fire crew's routine.

**Alternative fuel and electric vehicles.** High-voltage cables are typically orange. Do not cut them. Damaged lithium-ion battery packs can reignite hours later, so treat any electric vehicle fire as a fire department problem and keep your distance.

**Fuel and fluids.** Assume spilled liquid is flammable until fire says otherwise, and keep the area clear of ignition sources.

> **Key:** Simple access first, always. Then remove the vehicle from the patient, not the patient from the vehicle.

> **On the exam:** Rapid extrication has exactly three indications: unsafe scene, unstable patient, or the patient blocks access to a more critical patient.
keyPoints: Try simple access before any tool: doors, windows, unlocking, asking the patient.
Complex access is a fire department function; your job is the patient inside.
Remove the vehicle from the patient rather than pulling the patient out.
Rapid extrication has three indications: unsafe scene, unstable patient, or blocking access to a more critical patient.
Protect the patient from glass and noise, and never cut orange high-voltage cables on an electric vehicle.

checks.q: A stable patient is trapped in a car with a jammed driver's door. What should you try first?
choices: Request the hydraulic tool immediately
Try the other doors and windows for simple access
Break the driver's window at once
Perform rapid extrication
checks.why: Simple access costs seconds and frequently works, and glass and tools both add risk. Rapid extrication is reserved for an unsafe scene, an unstable patient, or a patient blocking access to someone sicker.

checks.q: Which situation justifies rapid extrication?
choices: The patient is anxious and wants out of the car
Fuel is leaking and pooling under the vehicle
The patient has an isolated ankle injury
Traffic is backing up behind the scene
checks.why: Pooling fuel makes the scene unsafe, which is one of the three indications. Anxiety, an isolated stable injury, and traffic congestion are not reasons to accept the added spinal risk.

lessons.title: Mass casualty incidents and the command system
lessons.body:
## What makes an incident an MCI

A **mass casualty incident (MCI)** is any incident where the number of patients exceeds the resources available. That is a relative definition on purpose. Four critical patients is an MCI for one ambulance and a routine afternoon for a large urban system.

The mental shift is the hardest part of EMS: you stop doing the most for each patient and start doing the most good for the most patients. The first arriving crew that kneels down and starts treating one screaming patient has just removed itself from the incident.

## What the first unit does

1. **Do not commit to patient care.**
2. Establish command and announce it on the radio, including a scene description and the estimated number of patients.
3. Request resources, generously and early. Ambulances, supervisors, fire, police, and a staging location.
4. Begin triage, or assign it.

The most valuable thing a first-arriving EMT does at an MCI is give an accurate, calm radio report and start sorting.

## The Incident Command System

ICS is the management structure inside the National Incident Management System (NIMS). Everyone uses the same structure so that agencies who have never worked together can plug into one organization.

**Incident Commander** runs the incident and owns every function not delegated. Command staff report directly to the IC:

- **Safety Officer**, the only person who can stop an unsafe operation immediately
- **Public Information Officer**, the single voice to media
- **Liaison Officer**, the contact point for outside agencies

General staff sections: **Operations** (does the tactical work), **Planning** (tracks status and builds the plan), **Logistics** (gets the stuff), and **Finance/Administration** (tracks the cost).

## The EMS functions you will actually be assigned

- **Triage:** sorts every patient and tags them
- **Treatment:** runs the color-coded treatment areas, red, yellow, and green, where care is given while patients wait for transport
- **Transport:** decides who leaves, on what, to where. Tracks each patient and destination, and spreads patients across hospitals so one facility is not overwhelmed
- **Staging:** holds incoming units and assigns them as requested, so arriving ambulances do not clog the scene
- **Rehab:** rest, hydration, and medical monitoring for responders

## Span of control and unified command

**Span of control** is the number of people one supervisor directs, and the workable range is **3 to 7, with 5 as the target**. Beyond that, people stop being supervised. When a section grows past it, you divide and add a supervisor.

**Single command** means one agency, one Incident Commander. **Unified command** is used when multiple agencies or jurisdictions share responsibility, such as a highway crash involving fire, EMS, state police, and a hazmat team. The agencies command jointly, share one set of objectives, and speak with one voice. It is not command by committee; it is one plan built by the people who each own a piece of the problem.

> **Key:** The first unit's job at an MCI is command, a resource request, and triage, not patient care.

> **On the exam:** Span of control is 3 to 7. The Safety Officer can stop operations. Unified command is for multi-agency incidents.
keyPoints: An MCI is any incident where patient numbers exceed available resources, which is relative to your system.
The first arriving unit establishes command, requests resources, and starts triage instead of treating.
ICS command staff are Safety, Public Information, and Liaison; general staff are Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance.
EMS functions are triage, treatment, transport, staging, and rehab.
Span of control is 3 to 7 with 5 as the target; unified command covers multi-agency incidents.

checks.q: You are the first ambulance at a crash with eight patients. What is your first action?
choices: Begin treating the most critical patient you can see
Establish command, give a scene report with patient count, and request resources
Load the two nearest patients and transport
Wait for a supervisor to arrive and assign you
checks.why: Committing the first crew to one patient removes the only person who can organize the scene. Command, an accurate count, and an early resource request are what get eight patients transported.

checks.q: Which ICS position has the authority to halt an unsafe operation immediately?
choices: Safety Officer
Public Information Officer
Logistics Section Chief
Transport Officer
checks.why: The Safety Officer is specifically empowered to stop or alter unsafe activity without going through the chain. The PIO handles media, Logistics obtains resources, and Transport moves patients.

checks.q: A treatment officer is directly supervising 14 providers. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, more supervision is better
Span of control is exceeded; the group should be divided with added supervisors
Treatment should never have a supervisor
The transport officer should take over all 14
checks.why: Effective span of control is 3 to 7 with 5 as the target, and 14 means nobody is actually being supervised. The fix is to subdivide and add supervisors, not to shift the whole group elsewhere.

lessons.title: START and JumpSTART triage
lessons.body:
## Thirty seconds per patient, two interventions only

**START** stands for Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment. It sorts adults and children roughly 8 and older into four categories in about 30 seconds each. During triage you perform exactly **two** interventions: open an airway by positioning, and control major bleeding. Nothing else. No CPR, no oxygen, no splints. Every extra minute you spend on one patient is a minute stolen from everyone you have not reached.

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Red, immediate | Life threat that is correctable; transport first |
| Yellow, delayed | Serious but can wait; transport after the reds |
| Green, minor | Walking wounded |
| Black, expectant | Dead, or injuries incompatible with survival given available resources |

## The START algorithm

**Step 1: Clear the walking wounded.** Announce loudly: "If you can hear me and you are able to walk, move to the sidewalk by the blue truck." Everyone who walks there is **green**. This can remove half your patient count in 20 seconds. Assign someone to watch them, because greens deteriorate and greens wander off.

**Step 2: Assess everyone remaining, one at a time, using RPM.**

**R, respirations.**
- Not breathing? Open the airway by positioning. If they start breathing, **red**. If they still do not breathe, **black**.
- Breathing faster than **30 per minute**, **red**.
- Breathing at 30 or less, move to perfusion.

**P, perfusion.**
- **Radial pulse absent**, or capillary refill **longer than 2 seconds**, **red**. Control major bleeding now.
- Radial pulse present, move to mental status.

**M, mental status.**
- Cannot follow a simple command such as "squeeze my hand", **red**.
- Follows commands, **yellow**.

So the only path to yellow is: breathing at 30 or less, radial pulse present, and following commands. Everything else in the non-ambulatory group is red or black.

## JumpSTART for children

Children about 1 to 8 years old get **JumpSTART**, which exists because children arrest from respiratory causes and will often restart with a few breaths. The differences:

1. **Apneic child:** open the airway. If breathing starts, **red**. If not, check a **peripheral pulse**. No pulse, **black**. Pulse present, give **5 rescue breaths**. If breathing starts, **red**. If still apneic, **black**.
2. **Respiratory rate:** the red thresholds are **under 15 or over 45** per minute, not over 30.
3. **Perfusion:** uses a **palpable peripheral pulse**, not capillary refill.
4. **Mental status:** uses **AVPU**. Alert, Verbal, or appropriate response to Pain is **yellow**. Inappropriate response to pain such as posturing, or Unresponsive, is **red**.

Infants too young to walk cannot be sorted by the walk test, so they are carried to the treatment area and triaged there.

## Tags and reassessment

Tag every patient, attach it where it will be seen, and do not re-triage a patient you already tagged unless their condition changes. Triage is dynamic: a yellow can become a red while waiting, so treatment areas reassess continuously.

> **Trap:** Black tags are the hardest thing in EMS and the most important discipline. In an MCI, resources spent on a pulseless patient are taken from patients who can be saved. The standard changes back the moment resources catch up.

> **On the exam:** Memorize the numbers. Over 30 breaths per minute is red, capillary refill over 2 seconds or absent radial pulse is red, cannot follow commands is red. JumpSTART is under 15 or over 45, with 5 rescue breaths for the apneic child with a pulse.
keyPoints: START sorts patients in about 30 seconds using only two interventions: open the airway and stop major bleeding.
Walking wounded are green; then RPM decides the rest.
Red triggers: apneic then breathing after positioning, rate over 30, absent radial pulse or cap refill over 2 seconds, cannot follow commands.
Yellow requires all three: rate 30 or less, radial pulse present, follows commands.
JumpSTART: rate under 15 or over 45 is red, uses peripheral pulse and AVPU, and gives 5 rescue breaths to an apneic child with a pulse.

checks.q: An adult at an MCI is breathing 36 times per minute with a strong radial pulse and follows commands. What tag?
choices: Green
Yellow
Red
Black
checks.why: A respiratory rate over 30 is an immediate red in START, and the algorithm stops there without checking perfusion or mental status. Good perfusion and intact mental status do not override the respiratory criterion.

checks.q: A 5-year-old is not breathing. You open the airway and she remains apneic, but she has a palpable pulse. What do you do?
choices: Tag black and move on
Give 5 rescue breaths; if she breathes, tag red; if not, tag black
Start full CPR
Tag yellow and reassess later
checks.why: JumpSTART adds the pulse check and 5 rescue breaths because pediatric arrest is usually respiratory and often reversible with a few breaths. Full CPR is outside the triage phase and would stop you from reaching other patients.

checks.q: During START triage you find a patient with severe arterial bleeding from the arm. What may you do?
choices: Nothing, triage does not include treatment
Control the bleeding, then continue triaging
Start an IV and give fluids
Splint the arm and apply oxygen
checks.why: Controlling major hemorrhage and opening an airway are the only two interventions permitted during triage, because both are seconds long and immediately lifesaving. Splints, oxygen, and IVs all belong in the treatment area.

lessons.title: Hazmat and WMD awareness
lessons.body:
## Awareness level means recognize and stay out

Most EMTs are trained to the **awareness level**, and its whole content is four verbs: **recognize** that hazardous materials are involved, **isolate** the area, **deny entry**, and **notify** the appropriate resources. You do not enter, you do not rescue, and you do not decontaminate. Patients come to you after decon.

This feels wrong when people are down in front of you. It is still correct: contaminated rescuers become contaminated patients, and a contaminated ambulance takes the emergency department offline.

## Recognizing it from a distance

Use binoculars and stay uphill, upwind, and upstream.

**Placards.** Transport vehicles carry diamond-shaped DOT placards showing a hazard class number 1 through 9 and often a four-digit UN identification number. Class 1 is explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids, 4 flammable solids, 5 oxidizers and organic peroxides, 6 poisons and infectious substances, 7 radioactive, 8 corrosives, 9 miscellaneous.

**Shipping papers.** In a truck they are in the cab with the driver; on a train the consist is with the conductor. They name the material precisely.

**The NFPA 704 diamond** marks fixed facilities, and you read it by position:

- **Blue, left:** health hazard
- **Red, top:** flammability
- **Yellow, right:** instability or reactivity
- **White, bottom:** special notices, where `W` with a slash means reacts with water, `OX` means oxidizer, and `SA` means simple asphyxiant

Blue, red, and yellow are rated `0` to `4`, where 0 is no hazard and 4 is severe.

**The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)** lives in every ambulance. Yellow pages look up materials by UN number, blue pages by name, orange pages give the action guide, and green pages give initial isolation and protective action distances for materials that are toxic by inhalation. For an unknown release, the general guidance is to isolate at least **330 feet, about 100 meters**, in all directions and increase from there.

## The three zones

- **Hot zone**, also called the exclusion zone: contamination is present. Only trained, properly protected personnel enter.
- **Warm zone**, the contamination reduction corridor: where decontamination happens.
- **Cold zone**: support, command, staging, treatment, and transport. This is where you work.

## Decontamination basics

**Gross decon** comes first and does most of the work: removing the patient's clothing eliminates roughly **80 to 90 percent** of the contaminant. Then a copious low-pressure water rinse, with soap for oily agents. Bag and label clothing and belongings. Trained teams run technical decon with separate ambulatory and non-ambulatory corridors.

Never bring an undeconned patient into the ambulance. Dry chemicals are brushed off before water is applied, because some react with it.

## Terrorism and WMD awareness

**CBRNE** covers Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, and Explosive threats.

Scene indicators that should make you stop: multiple patients with the **same symptoms and no trauma**, dead birds, insects, or animals, unexplained vapor clouds, odd odors, unattended packages or sprayers, a symbolic or crowded target, or a date with significance.

The rule that keeps responders alive is **secondary devices**. Attacks are deliberately designed to injure the people who respond, timed for arrival and often placed at the obvious staging point or command post. So: approach from upwind, do not cluster, avoid the obvious parking spot, look before you touch anything, and have police sweep before you commit crews.

Nerve agent exposure produces a recognizable picture remembered as **SLUDGEM**: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastrointestinal distress, Emesis, and Miosis, which is pinpoint pupils. Multiple patients with pinpoint pupils and wet everything is a nerve agent until proven otherwise, and the correct response is to back out and call for a hazmat response.

> **Key:** Recognize, isolate, deny entry, notify. Uphill, upwind, upstream. Patients after decon only.

> **On the exam:** NFPA 704 by position is blue health, red flammability, yellow instability, white special. Removing clothing removes 80 to 90 percent of contamination.
keyPoints: Awareness level is recognize, isolate, deny entry, notify; you never enter or decontaminate.
Stay uphill, upwind, and upstream, and use binoculars to read placards.
NFPA 704: blue health on the left, red flammability on top, yellow instability on the right, white special at the bottom, rated 0 to 4.
Zones are hot, warm for decon, and cold for treatment and transport; isolate at least 330 feet for an unknown release.
Removing clothing removes 80 to 90 percent of contamination; watch for secondary devices at terrorist incidents.

checks.q: You see an overturned tanker with a placard reading 1203 and a class 3 symbol. What is your first action?
choices: Approach to read the shipping papers
Stop uphill and upwind, isolate the area, deny entry, and notify hazmat
Begin decontaminating any patients you find
Enter and drag patients to safety
checks.why: Awareness level is recognize, isolate, deny entry, and notify, and class 3 is a flammable liquid. Approaching, entering, or attempting decon without training and protection turns rescuers into patients.

checks.q: On an NFPA 704 diamond, what does the blue section indicate?
choices: Flammability
Health hazard
Instability
Special hazards such as water reactivity
checks.why: Blue on the left is health, red on top is flammability, yellow on the right is instability, and white at the bottom carries special notices such as the water-reactive W.

checks.q: Six people at a train station have pinpoint pupils, drooling, vomiting, and no trauma. What should you suspect and do?
choices: Food poisoning; begin transporting patients
Nerve agent exposure; withdraw upwind, isolate, and request hazmat and law enforcement
Mass anxiety; reassure and release
Carbon monoxide; enter and ventilate the building
checks.why: Multiple patients with identical symptoms and no trauma, plus the SLUDGEM picture including miosis, is a chemical release until proven otherwise. Entering or transporting contaminated patients spreads the agent and disables your crew and receiving hospital.

lessons.title: Infection control, wellness, and reading the evidence
lessons.body:
## Standard precautions

You cannot tell who is infectious by looking, so you treat every patient's blood and body fluid as if it is. **Hand hygiene is the single most effective infection control measure there is.** Alcohol-based hand rub with 60 to 95 percent alcohol, rubbed until dry, roughly `20 seconds`. Soap and water for at least `20 seconds` whenever hands are visibly soiled, and specifically after caring for patients with Clostridioides difficile or norovirus, because alcohol does not kill those spores.

**Donning order:** gown, then mask or respirator, then eye protection, then gloves.
**Doffing order:** gloves, then eye protection, then gown, then mask or respirator, with hand hygiene after.

The logic is that the dirtiest item comes off first and the respiratory protection stays on longest.

An **N95 respirator** requires annual fit testing and a user seal check every single time. Facial hair breaks the seal. A surgical mask is not a respirator and does not protect against airborne disease such as tuberculosis or measles.

**Sharps:** never recap a needle, never hand a bare sharp to someone else, and dispose at the point of use in a puncture-resistant container. Most needlesticks happen during recapping or while walking with an uncapped needle.

**Cleaning:** use an EPA-registered disinfectant and honor the **contact time** printed on the label, which is usually a few minutes of visibly wet surface. Wiping and immediately drying does nothing. Clean high-touch surfaces after every call and do a full terminal clean per policy.

## After an exposure

1. **Wash immediately.** Soap and water on skin. Flush mucous membranes or eyes with water or saline for about `20 minutes`.
2. **Report immediately** to your designated infection control officer. Timing determines what treatment is possible, so this is not a shift-end task.
3. **Source testing and baseline labs** for you.
4. **Prophylaxis where indicated.** HIV post-exposure prophylaxis works best started within hours and no later than `72 hours`. Hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine are ideally given within `24 hours`.
5. **Follow-up testing** typically at 6 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months.

Approximate transmission risk from a single needlestick with an infected source: hepatitis B up to about `30%` in an unvaccinated person, hepatitis C about `1.8%`, HIV about `0.3%`. Hepatitis B is the most transmissible and the one you can prevent outright, which is why your employer must offer the three-dose vaccine series free under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.

## Provider wellness

Stress in EMS comes in three shapes: **acute** during the call, **delayed** days later, and **cumulative**, which becomes burnout. Warning signs include irritability, sleep changes, isolation, loss of interest, increased drinking, and cynicism about patients.

**Support:** peer support programs, employee assistance programs, and mental health professionals with first-responder experience. Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) offers defusings within hours and debriefings a day or three later. The evidence for mandatory single-session debriefing is mixed, so the current emphasis is voluntary peer support and real access to clinicians.

**Sleep and fatigue.** Fatigue impairs judgment and reaction time comparably to alcohol. Evidence-based EMS fatigue guidelines recommend shifts shorter than 24 hours where feasible, fatigue self-assessment tools, permitted napping on duty, and caffeine used strategically rather than constantly.

**The numbers that should get your attention:** EMS workers are injured on the job at roughly three times the rate of the average American worker, ground transportation crashes remain a leading cause of EMS line-of-duty deaths, and back injuries are the leading cause of career-ending disability. A widely cited 2015 survey of EMS providers found about 37 percent had contemplated suicide and 6.6 percent had attempted it, far above the general population.

## Public health and reading research

EMS is a public health service. **Primary prevention** stops the event, such as car seat and helmet programs. **Secondary prevention** catches disease early, such as blood pressure screening. **Tertiary prevention** limits disability after the fact, such as rehabilitation.

When you read a study, ask four questions: what kind of study is it, how many patients, was it randomized, and does the result apply to your patients? The strength ladder runs case report, case series, cohort or case-control, randomized controlled trial, then systematic review and meta-analysis at the top.

Two ideas worth carrying: a `p` value under `0.05` means the result is unlikely to be chance, not that it is clinically important; and correlation is not causation, which is why the observational studies supporting long-standing EMS practices keep collapsing when someone finally randomizes them.

> **Key:** Hand hygiene beats every other infection control measure. Report exposures immediately, because prophylaxis is time-sensitive.

> **On shift:** Emergency department techs handle more sharps than most EMTs. Set the container within arm's reach before the procedure starts, not after.
keyPoints: Hand hygiene is the most effective infection control measure; soap and water for visibly soiled hands and for C. difficile.
Don gown, mask, eye protection, gloves; doff gloves, eye protection, gown, mask, then hand hygiene.
Report exposures immediately: HIV prophylaxis within 72 hours, hepatitis B immune globulin ideally within 24 hours.
Needlestick risk is roughly 30 percent hepatitis B unvaccinated, 1.8 percent hepatitis C, 0.3 percent HIV.
Fatigue impairs like alcohol; back injuries and vehicle crashes are the leading career and life threats in EMS.

checks.q: What is the correct order for removing personal protective equipment?
choices: Mask, gown, eye protection, gloves
Gloves, eye protection, gown, mask, then hand hygiene
Gown, gloves, mask, eye protection
Eye protection, gloves, mask, gown
checks.why: The most contaminated item, gloves, comes off first and respiratory protection stays on longest, with hand hygiene at the end. Any order that removes the mask early exposes your airway while you are still handling contaminated equipment.

checks.q: You sustain a needlestick from a used IV catheter. What is the most time-critical action?
choices: Finish the call and report at the end of shift
Wash the site and report immediately so prophylaxis can be started
Squeeze the site to force out blood
Wait for the patient's lab results before reporting
checks.why: HIV prophylaxis is most effective within hours and useless after about 72 hours, so reporting is urgent. Delaying to the end of a shift or waiting on source results wastes the window, and squeezing the wound is not recommended.

checks.q: Which study design gives the strongest evidence for whether a treatment works?
choices: Case report
Case series
Randomized controlled trial or a systematic review of them
Expert opinion
checks.why: Randomization removes the confounding that makes observational data misleading, and systematic reviews pool multiple trials. Case reports, case series, and expert opinion generate hypotheses rather than confirming effect.

cards.front: What are the four national EMS certification levels?
cards.back: Emergency Medical Responder, EMT, Advanced EMT, and Paramedic. Each level adds skills to the one below it, and not every state uses AEMT.

cards.front: What separates an AEMT from an EMT?
cards.back: AEMTs add intravenous and intraosseous access, IV fluids, supraglottic airways, and a limited drug list. EMTs do not establish vascular access.

cards.front: What is a standing order?
cards.back: The part of a protocol you may perform without contacting a physician, such as oxygen for hypoxia or aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain. It is offline medical direction.

cards.front: Who defines your scope of practice versus your protocols?
cards.back: The state defines scope of practice, in New Jersey through the Office of EMS. Your physician medical director writes the protocols, which may restrict but never expand your scope.

cards.front: How is ALS delivered in New Jersey?
cards.back: By hospital-based Mobile Intensive Care Units staffed by Mobile Intensive Care Paramedics, responding in non-transporting fly cars that intercept the BLS ambulance.

cards.front: What is a just culture in EMS quality improvement?
cards.back: A system that separates human error and system problems, which get fixed, from reckless behavior, which gets disciplined. Punishing all errors means you stop hearing about them.

cards.front: What does staging mean and where do you do it?
cards.back: Waiting at a safe location until police declare the scene secure. Stage out of sight of the address, typically a block or more away, never in the driveway.

cards.front: How far from a downed power line must you stay?
cards.back: At least one full span, pole to pole, in every direction. Assume every wire is live until the utility company says otherwise, and never move a wire with any object.

cards.front: Where should you park at a roadway scene?
cards.back: About 100 feet before the scene, positioned so the ambulance shields the work area, with wheels turned away from responders. Wear an ANSI class 2 or higher high-visibility vest.

cards.front: What should occupants do when a live wire is on their vehicle?
cards.back: Stay inside. The vehicle body carries current around them, and any exit risks completing a circuit through the body or crossing an energized ground gradient.

cards.front: Name four indicators that a scene may turn violent.
cards.back: Pacing or clenched fists, someone positioning between you and the exit, escalating volume, a room that goes silent when you enter, visible weapons, or hands kept hidden.

cards.front: Does 'police on scene' mean the scene is safe?
cards.back: No. Ask specifically whether the scene is secure, and remember a cleared scene can turn unsafe again when a suspect or family member returns.

cards.front: Why does holding a load away from your body injure your back?
cards.back: Force on the lumbar discs multiplies with distance from the body. A 40-pound bag at arm's length loads the spine more than a heavier patient held close.

cards.front: Describe the power lift.
cards.back: Feet shoulder width and flat, back straight with its inward curve locked, bend at hips and knees, load close, lift with the legs, exhale on the lift, and never twist.

cards.front: What is a power grip?
cards.back: Palms up, hands about 10 inches apart, with the full palm and all fingers contacting the handle. Fingertip grips fail first under load.

cards.front: When is an emergency move indicated?
cards.back: Fire or explosion risk, uncontrolled hazardous materials, inability to protect the patient from hazards, inability to reach another patient needing lifesaving care, or a position preventing lifesaving care.

cards.front: What triggers an urgent move rather than an emergency move?
cards.back: The patient's condition rather than the scene: altered mental status, inadequate breathing, or shock. Rapid extrication from a vehicle is the classic example.

cards.front: Name the four common non-urgent moves.
cards.back: Direct ground lift, extremity lift, direct carry from bed to stretcher, and the draw sheet slide. The draw sheet is easiest on your back.

cards.front: What is the long backboard actually for?
cards.back: Movement and extrication, not treatment. Patients come off it promptly because it causes pressure injuries, pain, and restricted breathing.

cards.front: Which device do you use for a conscious patient going down stairs?
cards.back: A stair chair, with straps and a spotter below the crew. Never take a patient down stairs on a wheeled stretcher.

cards.front: What are the nine phases of an ambulance call?
cards.back: Preparation, dispatch, en route, arrival and size-up, transfer to the ambulance, transport, delivery, en route to station, and the post-run cleaning and restocking phase.

cards.front: At what pressure do you replace a portable oxygen cylinder?
cards.back: At or below 500 psi. A full D cylinder starts around 2000 psi, and suction should generate at least 300 mmHg.

cards.front: What is the legal standard for emergency vehicle operation?
cards.back: Due regard for the safety of all others. Lights and sirens grant exemptions from certain traffic laws but never immunity from liability.

cards.front: How much time does running lights and sirens actually save?
cards.back: Studies converge on roughly 1.7 to 3.6 minutes on a typical call, while crash risk rises substantially. That trade is a bad one for most patients.

cards.front: How do you handle an intersection during an emergency response?
cards.back: Come to a complete stop at every red light and stop sign, change the siren tone on approach, clear lane by lane with eye contact, and assume nobody hears you.

cards.front: What is the rule for backing an ambulance?
cards.back: Always use a spotter at the rear corner with agreed hand signals, and stop the moment you lose sight of them. With no spotter, get out and look before backing.

cards.front: What are the landing zone requirements for a medical helicopter?
cards.back: About 100 by 100 feet, firm and level with under about 8 degrees of slope, clear of wires, poles and debris, corners marked with weighted markers, loose items secured within 100 feet.

cards.front: How do you approach a helicopter safely?
cards.back: Only when the flight crew signals you, always from the front in the pilot's line of sight, never toward the tail rotor, and from the downhill side on a slope.

cards.front: What is the difference between simple and complex access?
cards.back: Simple access uses no tools: door handles, windows, unlocking, asking the patient. Complex access requires tools and training and belongs to the fire department.

cards.front: What are the three indications for rapid extrication?
cards.back: An unsafe scene, a patient whose condition requires immediate transport, or a patient blocking access to another more critically injured patient.

cards.front: What does 'remove the vehicle from the patient' mean?
cards.back: Disentangle by cutting the car away rather than dragging the patient through a small opening, so the patient can move in a straight line with the spine supported.

cards.front: How do you protect a patient while fire crews cut a vehicle?
cards.back: Manual in-line stabilization, a collar if indicated, eye and hearing protection, a heavy blanket or hard protection before glass breaks, and narrate each noise before it happens.

cards.front: What are the special hazards of electric and alternative fuel vehicles?
cards.back: High-voltage cables, usually orange, must never be cut, and damaged lithium-ion packs can reignite hours later. Treat any EV fire as a fire department problem.

cards.front: What is the definition of a mass casualty incident?
cards.back: Any incident where the number of patients exceeds the resources available. It is relative: four critical patients is an MCI for one ambulance.

cards.front: What does the first arriving unit do at an MCI?
cards.back: Does not commit to patient care. Establishes and announces command with a scene description and patient estimate, requests resources generously, and begins or assigns triage.

cards.front: Name the ICS command staff and general staff sections.
cards.back: Command staff: Safety Officer, Public Information Officer, Liaison Officer. General staff sections: Operations, Planning, Logistics, and Finance/Administration.

cards.front: What is span of control and what is the ideal number?
cards.back: The number of people one supervisor directs. The workable range is 3 to 7, with 5 as the target. Beyond that, subdivide and add supervisors.

cards.front: What is unified command and when is it used?
cards.back: Multiple agencies or jurisdictions commanding jointly under one set of objectives, used when fire, EMS, police, and others share responsibility for one incident.

cards.front: What does the transport officer do at an MCI?
cards.back: Decides who leaves, on which unit, and to which hospital, tracks every patient and destination, and spreads patients so no single facility is overwhelmed.

cards.front: What two interventions are allowed during START triage?
cards.back: Open the airway by positioning, and control major bleeding. Nothing else, because every extra minute is taken from patients you have not reached.

cards.front: What is the first step of START triage?
cards.back: Direct everyone who can walk to move to a designated area. All of them are tagged green, which can remove half your patient count in seconds.

cards.front: What does RPM stand for in START, and what are the red thresholds?
cards.back: Respirations, Perfusion, Mental status. Red if over 30 breaths per minute, if the radial pulse is absent or capillary refill exceeds 2 seconds, or if they cannot follow commands.

cards.front: In START, what happens to a patient who is not breathing?
cards.back: Open the airway by positioning. If they begin breathing, tag red. If they remain apneic, tag black. No CPR during triage.

cards.front: What three conditions must all be true for a yellow tag in START?
cards.back: Breathing at 30 or fewer per minute, radial pulse present with capillary refill under 2 seconds, and able to follow simple commands.

cards.front: What are the JumpSTART respiratory rate thresholds?
cards.back: Under 15 or over 45 breaths per minute is red. Between 15 and 45, move on to perfusion using a palpable peripheral pulse.

cards.front: How does JumpSTART handle an apneic child?
cards.back: Open the airway; if breathing starts, red. If not, check a peripheral pulse: no pulse is black; pulse present means give 5 rescue breaths, then red if breathing starts and black if not.

cards.front: How does JumpSTART assess mental status?
cards.back: With AVPU. Alert, Verbal, or an appropriate response to Pain is yellow. An inappropriate response to pain such as posturing, or Unresponsive, is red.

cards.front: What are the four actions at hazmat awareness level?
cards.back: Recognize that hazardous materials are involved, isolate the area, deny entry, and notify the appropriate resources. You do not enter, rescue, or decontaminate.

cards.front: How do you read an NFPA 704 diamond?
cards.back: By position: blue on the left is health, red on top is flammability, yellow on the right is instability, white at the bottom is special hazards. Colors are rated 0 to 4.

cards.front: What do the colored sections of the Emergency Response Guidebook contain?
cards.back: Yellow looks up materials by UN number, blue by name, orange gives the action guide, and green gives initial isolation and protective action distances for inhalation hazards.

cards.front: Name the three hazmat control zones.
cards.back: Hot or exclusion zone where contamination is present, warm zone which is the decontamination corridor, and cold zone for command, treatment, and transport.

cards.front: How much contamination does removing clothing eliminate?
cards.back: Roughly 80 to 90 percent. Gross decon by clothing removal comes first, then a copious low-pressure water rinse, with dry chemicals brushed off before water.

cards.front: What does SLUDGEM indicate and what should you do?
cards.back: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis, Miosis: nerve agent exposure. Back out upwind, isolate, and request hazmat and law enforcement.

cards.front: What is a secondary device and how do you guard against it?
cards.back: An explosive placed to injure responders, timed for their arrival and often at the obvious staging point. Approach upwind, do not cluster, avoid predictable parking, and have police sweep.

cards.front: What scene findings suggest a chemical or biological release?
cards.back: Multiple patients with the same symptoms and no trauma, dead birds or insects, unexplained vapor clouds, odd odors, unattended sprayers, or a symbolic target.

cards.front: What is the single most effective infection control measure?
cards.back: Hand hygiene. Alcohol rub of 60 to 95 percent rubbed until dry, or soap and water for at least 20 seconds when hands are soiled or after C. difficile or norovirus.

cards.front: What is the donning and doffing order for PPE?
cards.back: Don gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves. Doff gloves, eye protection, gown, mask or respirator, then perform hand hygiene.

cards.front: What is required to use an N95 respirator correctly?
cards.back: Annual fit testing and a user seal check every time. Facial hair breaks the seal, and a surgical mask is not a substitute for airborne protection.

cards.front: What is the time window for post-exposure prophylaxis?
cards.back: HIV prophylaxis works best within hours and no later than 72 hours. Hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine ideally within 24 hours. Report immediately, not at end of shift.

cards.front: What are the approximate needlestick transmission risks?
cards.back: Hepatitis B up to about 30 percent in an unvaccinated person, hepatitis C about 1.8 percent, HIV about 0.3 percent. Only hepatitis B is vaccine-preventable.

cards.front: Why does contact time matter when disinfecting the ambulance?
cards.back: EPA-registered disinfectants only kill organisms if the surface stays visibly wet for the labeled dwell time, usually a few minutes. Wiping and immediately drying does nothing.

cards.front: What are the three types of EMS stress?
cards.back: Acute during the call, delayed appearing days later, and cumulative, which becomes burnout. Warning signs include irritability, sleep change, isolation, and cynicism about patients.

cards.front: What are the three levels of prevention?
cards.back: Primary stops the event, such as helmet programs. Secondary catches disease early, such as blood pressure screening. Tertiary limits disability afterward, such as rehabilitation.

quiz.q: Which intervention is within the national EMT scope of practice?
choices: Starting an intravenous line
Manual defibrillation
Administering aspirin for suspected cardiac chest pain
Endotracheal intubation
quiz.why: Aspirin is a standard EMT medication under protocol. IV access begins at the AEMT level, and manual defibrillation and intubation are paramedic skills.

quiz.q: An EMT radios the emergency physician for permission to assist a patient with a medication not covered by protocol. This is an example of what?
choices: Offline medical direction
Online medical direction
A standing order
Scope of practice expansion
quiz.why: Live contact with a physician during a call is online medical direction. Protocols and standing orders are written in advance, and a physician order can never expand your state scope.

quiz.q: You are a BLS crew in New Jersey with a patient who needs cardiac monitoring, and the MICU is 10 minutes away while the hospital is 12 minutes away. What is the best action?
choices: Begin transport and arrange an intercept en route
Wait on scene for the MICU
Cancel the MICU and drive slowly
Have the MICU meet you at the hospital
quiz.why: New Jersey paramedics respond in non-transporting fly cars, so moving toward the hospital while arranging the intercept gives the patient both ALS and definitive care. Waiting burns minutes and meeting at the hospital wastes the intercept entirely.

quiz.q: Dispatch reports an assault with the assailant possibly still present. Police are 4 minutes out. What do you do?
choices: Respond to the scene and wait in the ambulance out front
Stage out of sight of the address until police confirm the scene is secure
Enter with your partner and stay near the door
Approach on foot to assess from a distance
quiz.why: Staging must be out of sight of the address, because the ambulance in front of the house is still on the scene and is a target. Entering or approaching on foot before police clear it puts the crew in the assailant's path.

quiz.q: At a highway crash, where should the ambulance be positioned and what should you wear?
choices: Past the scene in the fast lane, with a reflective jacket optional
Directly beside the wreck, no special clothing needed
About 100 feet before the scene to shield the work area, wearing an ANSI class 2 or higher vest
On the shoulder a quarter mile away with hazards on
quiz.why: Blocking upstream creates a protected work area, and high-visibility apparel is federally required on federal-aid highways. Parking beside the wreck removes the shield, and a quarter mile away is not a work area at all.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest is on a soft bed in a narrow bedroom. What move is appropriate and why?
choices: No move; begin compressions on the bed
Non-urgent direct carry after full assessment
Urgent move using a scoop stretcher
Emergency move to the floor, because the position prevents effective lifesaving care
quiz.why: Compressions on a soft surface are ineffective, and inability to provide lifesaving care in the current position is a listed indication for an emergency move. A scoop or a full assessment both cost time during an arrest.

quiz.q: Which action most increases the load on your lumbar spine during a lift?
choices: Holding the weight away from your body and twisting
Keeping the patient close to your body
Lifting with your legs
Counting the lift with your partner
quiz.why: Force on the discs rises with distance from the body and twisting under load shears the spine, which is the classic injury mechanism. Keeping the load close, lifting with the legs, and coordinating all reduce the risk.

quiz.q: You need to move a conscious, stable 240-pound patient from a second-floor apartment. Which is safest?
choices: Carry him down on the wheeled stretcher
Use a stair chair with a spotter below and request a lift assist
Have him walk down on his own without assistance
Perform an extremity lift down the stairs
quiz.why: A stair chair with a spotter is the designed tool for stairs, and knowing when to request extra hands is a skill, not a weakness. Wheeled stretchers are not carried down stairs and an extremity lift on a staircase is uncontrolled.

quiz.q: During the daily check you find the portable oxygen cylinder at 450 psi. What should you do?
choices: Leave it, since it still has pressure
Use it only for low-flow patients
Replace it, because 500 psi is the replacement threshold
Top it off from the onboard cylinder
quiz.why: At or below 500 psi the residual is unreliable for the duration of a call, so the cylinder is swapped. Reserving it for low-flow use or transfilling in the field are both unsafe improvisations.

quiz.q: Which statement about emergency vehicle operation is correct?
choices: Lights and sirens grant immunity from liability
Speed limits do not apply during transport
Right of way is automatically granted by law
The standard is due regard for the safety of others
quiz.why: Exemptions let you proceed after stopping, but you are judged against due regard if anything goes wrong. Right of way must be yielded to you, never taken, and no statute suspends safe speed.

quiz.q: Most ambulance collisions that occur while the vehicle is in reverse could be prevented by what?
choices: Using a spotter, or getting out and looking when none is available
Using lights and siren while backing
Backing faster to reduce exposure time
Relying on the backup camera alone
quiz.why: A spotter with agreed signals covers the blind zone a camera misses, and the driver stops the instant the spotter disappears from view. Lights and speed do nothing for a blind area behind the vehicle.

quiz.q: A helicopter is landing in a field you set up. Which action is correct?
choices: Approach as soon as the skids touch to save time
Wait for the crew's signal, then approach from the front in the pilot's view
Approach from the rear to stay out of the pilot's way
Approach from the uphill side on sloped ground
quiz.why: You approach only when signaled and only from the front, where the pilot can see you. The tail rotor is nearly invisible when spinning, and on a slope the main rotor dips toward the uphill side.

quiz.q: A patient is trapped in a vehicle with the driver's door jammed but the rear passenger door is unlocked and functional. What is the correct first step?
choices: Request hydraulic tools to open the driver's door
Break the driver's window
Enter through the rear door to reach and care for the patient
Perform rapid extrication immediately
quiz.why: Simple access is always attempted first, and a functioning door is the fastest, safest way to a patient. Tools and glass add risk and time when an opening already exists.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an indication for rapid extrication?
choices: The vehicle is on fire
The patient is unresponsive with inadequate breathing
The patient blocks access to a more critically injured passenger
The patient is stable but wants to get out quickly
quiz.why: Rapid extrication accepts added spinal risk and is justified only by scene danger, an unstable patient, or blocked access to someone sicker. Patient impatience is not a clinical indication.

quiz.q: You are the first unit at a school bus crash with roughly 20 patients. What do you do first?
choices: Establish command, report the scene and estimated patient count, and request resources
Begin treating the most seriously injured child
Load the two closest children and transport
Begin CPR on a pulseless patient
quiz.why: Committing the first crew to any single patient removes the only person able to organize the scene, and at an MCI a pulseless patient is triaged black. Command and an early resource request are what get twenty patients moved.

quiz.q: Which ICS function assigns arriving ambulances so they do not clog the scene?
choices: Triage
Treatment
Staging
Rehab
quiz.why: Staging holds incoming units at a designated location and releases them as the transport officer requests. Triage sorts patients, treatment cares for them in color-coded areas, and rehab supports responders.

quiz.q: A highway incident involves fire, EMS, state police, and a hazmat team. What command structure applies?
choices: Single command under the fire chief
Separate commands operating independently
No command needed for a highway incident
Unified command with shared objectives
quiz.why: Unified command lets agencies that each own part of the problem build one plan and speak with one voice. Independent commands produce conflicting orders, which is exactly what NIMS was designed to eliminate.

quiz.q: In START triage, a patient is breathing 22 per minute, has no radial pulse, and follows commands. What tag?
choices: Green
Yellow
Red
Black
quiz.why: An absent radial pulse fails the perfusion step, which makes the patient immediate regardless of the normal rate and intact mental status. Yellow requires all three steps to pass.

quiz.q: An adult at an MCI is apneic. You open the airway and he does not start breathing. What is the correct action?
choices: Tag black and move to the next patient
Begin rescue breathing
Begin CPR
Tag red and request a paramedic
quiz.why: In adult START, an apneic patient who does not breathe after airway positioning is tagged expectant, because resources spent there are taken from salvageable patients. Rescue breathing and CPR are JumpSTART and normal-operations responses, not adult triage steps.

quiz.q: Which finding requires an immediate red tag under JumpSTART but not under adult START?
choices: A respiratory rate of 12
A respiratory rate of 34
An absent radial pulse
Inability to follow commands
quiz.why: JumpSTART tags a rate under 15 as immediate because bradypnea in a child signals imminent arrest, while 12 passes the adult respiratory step. A rate of 34 is red in adults but acceptable under JumpSTART's 15 to 45 window.

quiz.q: Why is the walking-wounded step performed first in START?
choices: Walking patients are usually the sickest
It satisfies a legal requirement
It rapidly removes a large group from the assessment pool and identifies greens
It lets you delay calling for resources
quiz.why: One announcement can clear half the patient count in seconds and leaves you only the non-ambulatory patients to assess individually. Walking patients are by definition perfusing and oxygenating well enough to move.

quiz.q: An EMT trained to the hazmat awareness level arrives at a chemical release with patients down in the hot zone. What should the EMT do?
choices: Don a gown and gloves and retrieve the patients
Begin decontamination with a hose line
Enter briefly while holding a breath
Isolate the area, deny entry, and notify hazmat resources from a safe position
quiz.why: Awareness level authorizes recognizing, isolating, denying entry, and notifying, and nothing more. A gown and gloves offer no chemical protection, and a contaminated rescuer becomes a patient who also contaminates the ambulance and the hospital.

quiz.q: Where should you position yourself relative to an unknown chemical release?
choices: Uphill, upwind, and upstream at a distance, using binoculars
Downwind so you can smell the material and identify it
Directly adjacent to read the placard clearly
Downhill so vapors rise away from you
quiz.why: Vapors travel downwind, liquids run downhill, and many heavier-than-air gases pool low, so uphill and upwind is the only safe combination. Smelling a material to identify it is an exposure, not an identification method.

quiz.q: An NFPA 704 diamond shows a 4 in the red section. What does this indicate?
choices: Severe health hazard
Severe flammability hazard
Severe reactivity hazard
Water reactive
quiz.why: Red on top is flammability, and 4 is the most severe rating on the 0 to 4 scale. Health is blue on the left, instability is yellow on the right, and water reactivity appears as a slashed W in the white section.

quiz.q: After an explosion in a public building, what is the primary safety concern for arriving responders?
choices: Smoke inhalation
Secondary devices intended to injure responders
Traffic congestion
Media interference
quiz.why: Secondary devices are timed and placed specifically for responders, often at predictable staging points and command posts. Smoke, traffic, and media are real problems but none of them are engineered to kill the people who arrive to help.

quiz.q: You are removing PPE after caring for a patient with a suspected airborne infection. What comes off first and what comes off last?
choices: Mask first, gloves last
Gown first, gloves last
Eye protection first, gown last
Gloves first, respirator last
