quiz.why: The most contaminated item comes off first and respiratory protection stays on longest so your airway is protected while you handle contaminated equipment. Hand hygiene follows the entire sequence.

quiz.q: Which statement about post-exposure management after a needlestick is correct?
choices: Reporting can wait until the end of shift
HIV prophylaxis is most effective within hours and should begin no later than 72 hours
Only hepatitis C has a vaccine
Baseline testing is unnecessary if you feel well
quiz.why: Prophylaxis is time-critical, which is why exposures are reported immediately rather than at shift end. Hepatitis B, not C, is the vaccine-preventable one, and baseline testing establishes whether any later infection came from this exposure.

quiz.q: A study reports that patients who received a treatment had better outcomes, but patients were not randomly assigned. What is the main limitation?
choices: The sample was too large
Observational studies are never publishable
The p value cannot be calculated without randomization
Confounding may explain the association, so correlation does not prove causation
quiz.why: Without randomization, sicker or healthier patients may have been selected for treatment, which is exactly how many long-standing EMS practices survived until trials overturned them. Observational studies are valuable for generating hypotheses and can still report statistics.

scenarios.title: MCI: charter bus into a bridge abutment
scenarios.intro: At 0715 a charter bus carrying a college team leaves the roadway and strikes a bridge abutment on a state highway. You are the first BLS ambulance on scene. Fire is 6 minutes out, state police are arriving, and dispatch has no patient count. The bus is upright, off the travel lanes, with no fire and no fluid leaking. People are climbing out of the front door and standing in the grass.

steps.prompt:
You pull up. You can see at least a dozen people out of the bus and more inside.

What is your first action?

choices.text: Grab the jump bag and start treating the person screaming loudest
choices.feedback: The loudest patient is almost never the sickest, and the first unit that commits to one patient removes the only person who can organize this scene.

choices.text: Establish command on the radio, describe the scene, estimate patient count, and request a large resource assignment plus a staging location
choices.feedback: Correct. The most valuable thing the first EMT does at an MCI is a calm, accurate radio report and a generous early resource request. You can always cancel units.

choices.text: Start loading the two most obviously injured people and transport
choices.feedback: That removes your ambulance and your crew from the scene before anyone knows how many patients exist. It also guarantees the sickest patients are found by somebody else, later.

choices.text: Wait for a supervisor to arrive and assign you a role
choices.feedback: Command exists from the moment the first unit arrives. Waiting means nobody is counting patients, requesting resources, or sorting for the next six minutes.

steps.prompt:
You have declared an MCI and requested 8 ambulances, 2 supervisors, fire, and a staging location at the shopping center a quarter mile back.

You are about to start triage. What do you announce first?

choices.text: "If you can hear my voice and you are able to walk, move to the grass by the blue road sign."
choices.feedback: Correct. The walking wounded step can clear half the patient count in twenty seconds, and everyone who walks there is a green. Assign someone to watch them so they do not wander or deteriorate unnoticed.

choices.text: "Everyone stay exactly where you are and wait for us."
choices.feedback: You just kept your green patients mixed in with the reds, and you now have to assess every one of them individually. START starts with the walk test for a reason.

choices.text: Nothing; begin assessing patients one by one starting at the front of the bus
choices.feedback: Assessing sequentially without clearing the ambulatory group wastes your scarcest resource, which is your own time. You could spend ten minutes on people who would have walked away.

steps.prompt:
Fourteen people walk to the grass. Six patients remain, all non-ambulatory. Triage them using START. You have tags, gloves, and 30 seconds each.

**Patient A:** on the floor of the aisle, not breathing. You open the airway by positioning and he begins breathing at about 24 per minute.
**Patient B:** seated, breathing 38 per minute, radial pulse present, answers questions.

What tags?

choices.text: A red, B red
choices.feedback: Correct on both. A is red because he only breathes after you opened the airway. B is red on the respiratory step alone, since anything over 30 per minute stops the algorithm right there.

choices.text: A black, B yellow
choices.feedback: Both wrong. A started breathing after positioning, which is an immediate red, not a black. B is over 30 per minute, which is red regardless of pulse and mental status.

choices.text: A red, B yellow
choices.feedback: A is right. B is not: a respiratory rate of 38 exceeds 30, and START stops at the first failed step. Being able to answer questions does not override the respiratory criterion.

choices.text: A yellow, B red
choices.feedback: B is right. A is not: a patient who was apneic and breathes only after you positioned the airway is immediate, because that airway will close again the moment nobody is holding it.

steps.prompt:
**Patient C:** on the floor, breathing 20 per minute, no radial pulse, capillary refill about 4 seconds, with a bleeding thigh laceration.
**Patient D:** slumped in a seat, breathing 16 per minute, radial pulse present, does not respond to "squeeze my hand."

What tags, and what are you allowed to do?

choices.text: C red with direct pressure or a tourniquet applied, D red; airway positioning and bleeding control are the only interventions allowed
choices.feedback: Correct. C fails perfusion and D fails mental status, so both are immediate. Controlling major bleeding is one of the two permitted triage interventions and takes seconds.

choices.text: C red, D yellow, and start oxygen on both
choices.feedback: D cannot follow a simple command, which is an immediate red. Oxygen is not a triage intervention; only airway positioning and hemorrhage control are permitted.

choices.text: C yellow because she is breathing normally, D red
choices.feedback: D is right. C is not: an absent radial pulse with a capillary refill of 4 seconds fails the perfusion step, and START stops at the first failure.

choices.text: C red with bleeding controlled, D red, and begin a full assessment on C
choices.feedback: Tags are right and the bleeding control is right, but stopping for a full assessment on C halts triage. Two patients are still unsorted and you are the only one sorting.

steps.prompt:
**Patient E:** on the floor near the rear, not breathing. You open the airway by positioning. He remains apneic.
**Patient F:** trapped under a seat frame, breathing 18 per minute, radial pulse strong, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert, follows commands, complaining of severe leg pain.

What tags?

choices.text: E black, F yellow
choices.feedback: Correct, and both are hard for different reasons. E is expectant under adult START because apnea persisting after airway positioning means no resources are spent there. F passes all three steps, so despite pain and entrapment he is delayed.

choices.text: E red and begin CPR, F red because he is trapped
choices.feedback: CPR is not part of triage, and starting it commits your entire crew to one expectant patient while five salvageable patients wait. Entrapment by itself does not change a triage category.

choices.text: E black, F red because of severe pain
choices.feedback: E is right. Pain does not upgrade a triage category. F passes respirations, perfusion, and mental status, which is the definition of delayed. His extrication is a resource question, not a triage question.

steps.prompt:
Final count: 14 green, 4 red, 1 yellow, 1 black. Fire has arrived and is working on Patient F's entrapment. Four ambulances are in staging. The nearest trauma center is 18 minutes away and takes up to 2 critical patients at once; a community hospital is 7 minutes away.

Command asks you to brief the incoming transport officer. What is the correct plan?

choices.text: Send all four reds to the trauma center so they get the highest level of care
choices.feedback: That overwhelms one facility, and a hospital that is saturated becomes slower than a closer one that is not. Transport officers deliberately distribute patients.

choices.text: Transport reds first, distributed across facilities so no hospital is overloaded; the yellow goes after the reds; track every patient and destination
choices.feedback: Correct. Reds first, spread across facilities, with a written track of who went where on which unit. The tracking is what lets families and hospitals find people afterward.

choices.text: Transport the 14 greens first since they are ready to go and will clear the scene
choices.feedback: Backwards. Greens are last precisely because they can wait, and sending them first consumes every ambulance you have while four immediate patients sit on the grass.

choices.text: Send everyone to the closest hospital to minimize transport time
choices.feedback: A 7-minute community hospital cannot absorb four critical trauma patients, and each one would need a second transfer. Distribution by capability and capacity is the transport officer's entire job.

scenarios.debrief: Two things decide an MCI, and neither is clinical skill. The first is that the first arriving unit commands, counts, and requests instead of treating. The second is triage discipline: 30 seconds per patient, only two interventions, and tags that follow the algorithm rather than your instincts. Run START in order and stop at the first failed step. Walking means green. Apnea that resolves with airway positioning is red; apnea that does not is black. Over 30 breaths per minute is red. Absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds is red. Cannot follow commands is red. Only the patient who passes all three steps is yellow. Notice what never changes a category: pain, entrapment, how loud someone is, how young they are, or how much you want to help them. Notice too that triage is dynamic, so treatment areas reassess continuously, and a yellow waiting on the grass can become a red in ten minutes.

scenarios.title: Hazmat: overturned tanker on a county road
scenarios.intro: At 1340 you are dispatched for a single-vehicle crash with injuries on a rural county road. Dispatch says a tractor-trailer is on its side. It is a clear day with a light steady wind out of the west. As you approach from the east, you can see the tanker lying across both lanes with a visible pool spreading from the trailer and a faint haze above it. A man is waving at you from the ditch about 50 feet from the trailer, and someone appears to be lying in the grass beyond him.

steps.prompt:
You are about 400 feet from the tanker, approaching from the east. The wind is from the west, which means it is blowing from the tanker toward you.

What do you do?

choices.text: Continue to the scene and check the man in the ditch first
choices.feedback: You would be driving downwind into a vapor haze from an unknown product. The waving man is not necessarily the sickest patient, and you cannot help anyone from inside the cloud.

choices.text: Stop, back away, reposition uphill and upwind, and keep at least several hundred feet of distance
choices.feedback: Correct. Vapors travel downwind and liquids run downhill. Repositioning costs a minute and is the difference between being a responder and being a patient.

choices.text: Drive past quickly to get upwind on the far side
choices.feedback: Driving through the release to get around it exposes you and the ambulance to the product. Back out the way you came in, which is the only route you know is clean.

choices.text: Park where you are and wait for fire to tell you what to do
choices.feedback: Better than driving in, but you are still downwind of an unknown release and you have not isolated anything or given a report. Reposition first, then report.

steps.prompt:
You are now uphill and upwind, about 800 feet out. Through binoculars you can read a diamond placard on the trailer: a four-digit number `1017` above a green-and-white symbol you cannot make out clearly, and the number `2` at the bottom of the diamond.

What do you do with this information?

choices.text: Look up the UN number in the yellow section of the Emergency Response Guidebook and read the assigned orange guide page
choices.feedback: Correct. Yellow pages index by UN number, blue by name, orange gives the action guide, and green gives isolation distances for inhalation hazards. Class 2 is a gas.

choices.text: Approach closer to read the shipping papers in the cab
choices.feedback: Shipping papers are in the hot zone. You have a UN number, which is enough to look up the product from where you are standing.

choices.text: Assume it is fuel and set up a landing zone
choices.feedback: Assumption is the enemy here. The placard gives you a specific identification, and setting up a landing zone near an unidentified gas release without knowing distances is premature.

steps.prompt:
The guidebook identifies the material as chlorine, a toxic gas that is heavier than air, and directs you to the green pages for initial isolation and protective action distances.

What does that change?

choices.text: Nothing; you are already far enough away at 800 feet
choices.feedback: For a toxic-inhalation-hazard material the green pages can call for downwind protective action measured in fractions of a mile or more, particularly for a large release. Read the distance, do not assume it.

choices.text: Expand the isolation distance per the green pages, stay uphill and upwind, avoid low ground because the gas is heavier than air, and pass the product name and distances to incoming units and dispatch
choices.feedback: Correct. A heavier-than-air gas collects in ditches, culverts, and basements, which is exactly where patients and responders end up standing.

choices.text: Move to the low ground so the gas passes overhead
choices.feedback: Backwards and dangerous. Chlorine is denser than air and pools in low areas, so the ditch is the worst place on this scene.

steps.prompt:
The man who was waving has now walked up the hill toward you. He is coughing hard, his eyes are streaming, and his clothes are damp. He is about 30 feet from your ambulance and closing.

What do you do?

choices.text: Bring him into the ambulance and start oxygen immediately
choices.feedback: That contaminates your patient compartment, your crew, and eventually the emergency department. A contaminated ambulance is out of service and the hospital may have to close its doors.

choices.text: Stop him at a distance, direct him to remove his outer clothing and move further upwind, and have decon set up before any hands-on care
choices.feedback: Correct. Removing clothing is gross decon and eliminates roughly 80 to 90 percent of contaminant. He walked to you, so he is ambulatory decon, and you treat after decon, not before.

choices.text: Put on a gown and gloves and assess him where he stands
choices.feedback: A gown and exam gloves are not chemical protection and do nothing against a vapor. Awareness level means you do not make contact with a contaminated patient.

choices.text: Tell him to sit down and wait, and go check the person lying in the grass
choices.feedback: The person in the grass is inside the hot zone, in a heavier-than-air toxic gas, and reaching them requires protection and training you do not have. Entering would add two patients, not subtract one.

steps.prompt:
Fire arrives and establishes hazmat operations. They set the hot zone boundary at the base of the hill, the warm zone with a decon corridor halfway up, and ask you to establish the cold zone functions.

Where do you set up and what do you do?

choices.text: In the cold zone: a treatment area, staging for incoming ambulances, and a transport function, receiving patients only after decon
choices.feedback: Correct. Cold zone holds command, treatment, staging, and transport. Every patient crosses the decon corridor before any EMS hands touch them.

choices.text: In the warm zone, so you can start care as soon as patients come off the line
choices.feedback: The warm zone is the contamination reduction corridor and requires protective equipment and training you do not have. EMS works in the cold zone.

choices.text: At the hot zone boundary so you can see everything
choices.feedback: Standing at the hot zone line puts you inside the vapor plume's variable edge, and plume edges move with the wind. That is not an operating position, it is an exposure.

steps.prompt:
Two decontaminated patients are delivered to your treatment area, both coughing with burning eyes and throats. A television crew has arrived at the intersection behind you and a reporter approaches your ambulance asking you what the chemical is and how many people are hurt.

What is correct?

choices.text: Tell her it is chlorine and give the patient count you have
choices.feedback: Not your role. Releasing incident and patient information to media outside the ICS structure risks wrong numbers, patient privacy, and contradicting command.

choices.text: Refer her to the Public Information Officer or Incident Command, and continue caring for your patients
choices.feedback: Correct. The PIO is the single voice to media under ICS, which is what keeps the public information accurate and keeps patient information private.

choices.text: Tell her you cannot say anything at all and walk away without explanation
choices.feedback: The instinct to decline is right but pointing her to the PIO takes two seconds and is better for everyone, including the public who needs shelter-in-place instructions.

choices.text: Let one of the patients speak to her since it is their own story
choices.feedback: A patient in your care, just decontaminated and symptomatic, is not in a position to consent meaningfully, and facilitating it makes you part of the disclosure.

scenarios.debrief: Hazmat awareness is almost entirely about what you do not do. You recognize, isolate, deny entry, and notify. You stay uphill, upwind, and upstream, and you identify the product from a distance using the placard's UN number, the NFPA 704 diamond at a fixed facility, or shipping papers that someone else retrieves. The Emergency Response Guidebook does the rest: yellow by number, blue by name, orange for the action guide, green for isolation and protective action distances on toxic-inhalation materials. Three specific traps show up in this case. A heavier-than-air gas pools in the low ground, which is where the instinct to take cover sends you. An ambulatory contaminated patient will walk straight to your ambulance, and letting him in takes your unit and possibly the receiving hospital out of service, so clothing comes off before care goes on. And the person lying in the grass inside the hot zone is not your rescue, no matter how visible they are; entering without protection and training adds patients rather than saving one. EMS works in the cold zone, treats after decon, and sends the media to the Public Information Officer.
